name: David Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Kindred Home Care, a small family firm in our market town, run by Mr and Mrs Okafor. I do the rural round, so I'm driving between farms and villages, about fifty miles a day. Mornings are getting people up and washed, then lunches, and the evenings are tea and bed. I've been with them since I was twenty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the old farmers, like Mr Whitaker, who's eighty-eight and still tells me how to drive. What wears me out is the winter roads and the calls that run over. With the mileage and the weekend rate I'm on decent money, and I've got about ten months' wages saved. My fiancée Ana and I are getting married next June, so every pound has a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd have guessed anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed it in the first place, and I'd say it at Sunday lunch to anyone listening. At work Mrs Okafor would probably agree with me, she doesn't trust computers either. I'm not online much, so that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes, and that's what I want. The wedding's booked, Ana and I are looking at houses, and my job's steady. The only worry I'd have is the roads in winter and the price of diesel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the rural round and the weekends. Ana and I would go ahead and buy a house after the wedding, probably the spring after. Maybe I'd ask the Okafors for a few more hours to build the deposit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the price of diesel. How much does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than people think. I get mileage, but it doesn't keep up when prices jump, and fifty miles a day adds up. Last winter I lost about forty a month on fuel compared with the rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI touch anything at Kindred, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the office, because Mrs Okafor's daughter does the rota on the computer. But she'd do it the same way, just quicker. Out on the rural round, nothing would change, and my client Mr Whitaker would still want his porridge thick.

say: I'd say I **never believed** the AI hype in the first place.
I'd say it at **Sunday lunch**, since I'm hardly online.
think: Nothing changing is **what I want**, with the wedding booked.
My only worries are **winter roads** and diesel prices.
do: Keep doing the **rural round** and the weekend shifts.
Buy a **house with Ana** in the spring after the wedding.
Ask the owners for **more hours** to build the deposit faster.
S0.quote: Out on the rural round, nothing would change, and my client Mr Whitaker would still want his porridge thick.
fieldNote: His life plan, **wedding then house**, runs smoothly in this picture.
His real money gripe is **fuel costs** outpacing the mileage rate.
He shares his employer's **distrust of computers** and is barely online.

steps.text: Keep doing the rural round and the weekend shifts
Buy a house with Ana in the spring after the June wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office types get it. That's what I always said would happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, you can't replace a pair of hands and a kind word. At church people would ask me about it and I'd tell them care is safe. I'd say the government should make sure jobs go to people first, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm fine. The paperwork and the rota might go on a computer, and Mrs Okafor's daughter would deal with that. I'd still be driving out to Mr Whitaker's every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the round, same as now. If they bring in some app for notes, I'd do the minimum, and if it got bad, I'd look at other agencies, there's plenty round here. The wedding and house would go ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Slightly annoyed at all the fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the minimum on any app. What if the agency insists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, but I wouldn't like it. I'd get Ana to show me, she's better with that stuff from the school. I'm not going to lose a good job over a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you know who'd feel this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Rafael works in a bank call centre in the city. That's exactly what's on your card, answering customers. My aunt would be worried sick, and I'd tell him to come and do care, honestly.

say: I'd say you can't replace a **pair of hands** and a kind word.
I'd say the government should put **jobs for people** before machines.
think: The **paperwork and rota** might go on a computer, which isn't my job.
I'd still be **driving out** to my clients every morning.
do: Keep the **round** the same as now.
Do the **minimum** on any app, with Ana's help.
Go ahead with the **wedding and house**.
feel: **Fine**, and a bit annoyed at the fuss.
S1.quote: You can't replace a pair of hands and a kind word.
fieldNote: He feels **safe** because his work is hands-on and the office handles tech.
His worry goes to his cousin **Rafael** in a bank call centre.
His traditional view shows in wanting government to **put people first**.

steps.text: Keep the same rural round of morning and evening calls
Wait to see if the agency brings in a notes app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And robots that can do my job by 2031? That's when we'd want our first baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has gone too far and somebody has to stop it, and I'd say it loudly at church and at the pub. I'd blame the big tech firms and the politicians who let them. Care for the old is a family's job and a community's job, not a machine's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Kindred would hold out a bit, because the Okafors are old-fashioned, but the council contracts would go to whoever's cheapest. If a robot does my round for half the price, the agency loses the contract and I lose my job. That would be around the time Ana and I would want children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house hunt and keep the wedding small, maybe the church hall instead of the hotel. I'd put every spare pound into savings, and we might move in with Ana's parents for a year to build it up. And I'd vote for whoever promises to keep people in care work, and I'd tell everyone I know to do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. Angry too, but mostly frightened for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on, so the thinking AI arrives in 2028 and robots for hands-on work around 2031. What do those three years mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're three years of knowing it's coming and not being able to stop it. The office would change first, the rota and the notes, but I'd still be driving to the farms. I'd use the time to save, but I don't know what I'd switch to, I've only ever done care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on Ana's parents. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great. I was raised that a man provides for his own house. But that's what family's for, and her dad would rather we were under his roof than in debt.

say: I'd say AI has **gone too far** and someone has to stop it.
I'd **blame big tech** and the politicians who let them.
think: Council contracts would go to the **cheapest robot**, and my agency would lose out.
Losing my job would hit right when we'd want **children**.
do: Stop the **house hunt** and hold a small church hall wedding.
Move in with **Ana's parents** for a year to save.
Vote for whoever will **keep people in care** work.
feel: **Frightened** for his household, with anger underneath.
S2.quote: If a robot does my round for half the price, the agency loses the contract and I lose my job.
fieldNote: The robot date of **2031** collides with his plans for a first child.
He blames **big tech and politicians**, and sees care as a family duty.
Leaning on **in-laws** clashes with his belief that a man provides.

steps.text: Put the house hunt on hold and hold the wedding in the church hall
Move in with Ana's parents for a year to build savings
Vote for candidates who promise to keep people in care work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots in 2034. A bit more room, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, that care should stay human, but I'd be less shouty about it. At church I'd say we need to look after each other, because the government won't. I'd still blame the tech companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it gives Ana and me time to get married, buy something small and maybe have a baby before it hits. But by 2034 I'd still expect my round to be gone. I'd be thirty-five with a family and no trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a small house, smaller than we wanted, and overpay it. I'd keep doing care, saving hard, and see whether the Okafors keep their contracts through 2031. I wouldn't jump into something new until I could see what's actually left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less frightened than with the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years, compared with the fast one, change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between starting a family and putting it off. With five years, I think we'd have our first before the robots come. I'd rather face the robots as a dad with a house than as a lodger at my in-laws.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see what's left. Wouldn't five years be time to learn a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. My uncle Tiago's a plumber and he's said before I could go with him. But robots would come for plumbing too, wouldn't they, so I'd only be swapping one worry for another.

say: I'd say **care should stay human**, but less loudly.
I'd tell church friends we must **look after each other**.
think: Five years gives time to marry, buy and maybe **have a baby**.
By **2034** I'd expect my round gone, with a family and no trade.
do: Buy a **smaller house** and overpay it.
**Wait** to see what's left before jumping into something new.
feel: **Worried**, but less frightened than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: I'd rather face the robots as a dad with a house than as a lodger at my in-laws.
fieldNote: The extra years mean **starting a family** rather than postponing it.
He dismisses **plumbing with his uncle** because robots would come for it too.
Resistance shows in waiting until he can **see what's left**.

steps.text: Buy a smaller house than planned and overpay the mortgage
Save hard from the care wage through 2031
Watch whether the agency keeps its council contracts before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036, and robots in 2039. I'd be forty, with kids at school, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty of things never happen. At church and at work I'd say we'll cross that bridge. I'd still say families should be caring for their own, robot or no robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd half not believe it. Ten years out, people say all sorts. But if it's true, I'd have my best working years in care before it hits, and that's not bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with everything: the wedding, the house in the spring and trying for children. I'd keep the rural round and maybe take the senior carer job if the Okafors offer it. I wouldn't change anything just yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A little shadow, but a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When the thinking AI arrives in 2036, the rota and care notes go first. What would that do to a small firm like Kindred?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Okafors might finally get rid of the paper rota, and good luck to them. It'd probably save the office some hours. Out on the round I'd be the same until the robots come, so three more years of farms and porridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything with the ten years that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have children without worrying, mainly. With ten years, my kids would be at school before any robot could do my round. That's a different feeling altogether.

say: I'd say ten years is long and **plenty never happens**.
I'd say families should **care for their own**, robot or no robot.
think: I'd **half not believe** a forecast ten years out.
I'd get my **best working years** in care before it hits.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding, house** and trying for children.
Keep the **rural round** and take senior carer if offered.
feel: **Pretty calm**, with a small shadow a long way off.
S4.quote: With ten years, my kids would be at school before any robot could do my round.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **keep every plan** he already had.
He doubts **long-range forecasts**, which suits his wish not to change.
He'd welcome the end of the **paper rota** as long as the round stays.

steps.text: Marry Ana next June and buy the house the following spring
Keep the rural round and take a senior carer post if offered

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. It lands right on top of the wedding and the first baby. What would help is the government making sure care contracts go to firms that employ people, and a bit of time to plan. I don't want handouts, I want to keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of the people I care for want to pray with someone, or just have their hand held while the radio's on. A machine can hold a hand, but it can't pray with my client Mr Whitaker.

headlineQuote: Care for the old is a family's job and a community's job, not a machine's.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old rural carer** for a small family-run agency in a market town.
He's **engaged to Ana**, saving for a house, with about ten months' wages put by.
He distrusts technology, **blames big tech** and politicians, and sees care as a family duty.
Fast AGI makes him **shelve the house** and move in with in-laws; a decade changes nothing.
He'd rather **wait and see** than retrain, even into a trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, landing on top of the wedding and the first baby.
whatWouldHelp: Care contracts going to **firms that employ people**.
**Time to plan** and keep working, rather than handouts.
